question: What is the main purpose of an Information Retrieval System in nursing?

options.A: To write nursing care plans without human input
options.B: To store, organize, and quickly find relevant clinical data
options.C: To automatically diagnose complex patient illnesses
options.D: To track daily hospital staff attendance records

explanation: An IRS is built specifically to help users locate stored information like research papers and clinical guidelines out of massive databases. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why are Information Retrieval Systems necessary for modern clinical practice?

options.A: The volume of medical knowledge is too large to memorize
options.B: Paper textbooks are completely banned in modern hospitals
options.C: Computers make fewer clinical mistakes than registered nurses
options.D: Patients demand to see database printouts during rounds

explanation: Medical and nursing knowledge grows rapidly, making digital search systems essential for accessing current facts instantly. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h1)

question: What is the document corpus in an Information Retrieval System?

options.A: The error log generated by failed searches
options.B: The search bar where the user types keywords
options.C: The total collection of stored documents and texts
options.D: The computer hardware holding the power supply

explanation: The corpus refers to the entire library or database of stored content that the system is able to search through. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h2)

question: Why do search engines use an index instead of reading every document from scratch every time?

options.A: To translate English articles into local languages
options.B: To prevent users from typing long sentences
options.C: To make the search process happen almost instantly
options.D: To permanently delete outdated nursing research articles

explanation: Indexing pre-processes the data so the system can locate matches in milliseconds rather than scanning every file line by line. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h2)

question: Which retrieval model strictly includes or excludes documents based on exact logic rules?
explanation: The Boolean model relies on strict true-or-false matching using logical operators like AND, OR, and NOT. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h3)

question: How does the Vector Space Model determine which documents are the best match?

options.A: By checking how many times the patient's name appears in the text
options.B: By calculating the mathematical overlap between search terms and document themes
options.C: By asking the original author of the paper to vote on its usefulness
options.D: By selecting files created on the same calendar day

explanation: The vector space model measures the closeness of keywords and document concepts in a mathematical space to rank results. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h3)

question: Which Boolean operator should you use when you want to broaden your search to include synonyms?
explanation: The OR operator tells the database to retrieve documents containing any of the listed terms, which expands your results. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h4)

question: A nurse wants to find articles about asthma in children, but wants to completely leave out studies on adults. Which search string is best?
explanation: Using AND narrows the focus to asthma and children, while NOT removes any articles that mention adults. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of MeSH terms in healthcare databases?

options.A: To calculate the financial cost of hospital research projects
options.B: To provide a standardized vocabulary for consistent article indexing
options.C: To automatically generate nursing care plans for patients
options.D: To translate clinical articles into multiple foreign languages

explanation: MeSH terms standardize medical concepts so that synonyms and different writing styles do not hide relevant articles from your search. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h5)

question: Why might a standard keyword search miss relevant articles that a MeSH search would easily find?

options.A: MeSH databases hide articles that were published before 1990
options.B: Authors use different words for the same clinical condition
options.C: Standard keywords are illegal to use in evidence-based practice
options.D: Computers cannot read lowercase letters in standard search bars

explanation: If an author uses 'heart attack' instead of 'myocardial infarction', a strict keyword search might miss it, whereas a MeSH term covers both. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h5)

question: What does 'precision' measure in an information retrieval search?

options.A: The percentage of articles written by registered nurses
options.B: The proportion of retrieved documents that are actually relevant
options.C: The total number of seconds the computer takes to search
options.D: The exact number of spelling errors found in the abstract

explanation: Precision evaluates how well your search weeded out useless results, telling you what percentage of what you found was truly useful. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h6)

question: What usually happens to your search precision when you broaden your search terms to increase recall?

options.A: Precision increases because the computer works twice as fast
options.B: Precision drops to zero because the system crashes immediately
options.C: Precision stays exactly the same regardless of search terms
options.D: Precision decreases because more irrelevant results get pulled in

explanation: There is a classic inverse relationship between precision and recall; casting a wider net brings in more noise along with the good articles. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h6)

question: What is the primary role of information retrieval systems in evidence-based nursing?

options.A: Replacing doctors during emergency resuscitation procedures
options.B: Recording patient vital signs directly into paper charts
options.C: Scheduling nursing shifts for weekend hospital coverage
options.D: Connecting clinical questions to published research evidence

explanation: IR systems give nurses rapid access to the research literature needed to support evidence-based clinical decisions. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h7)

question: A nurse wants to find the best evidence for managing pressure ulcers before updating the ward policy. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Throw away all current textbooks and rewrite the guidelines from memory
options.B: Formulate a clear clinical question and search a nursing database
options.C: Wait for a pharmaceutical company to mail a new brochure
options.D: Ask every patient on the ward what treatment they prefer

explanation: Evidence-based practice starts by defining the question and using an IR system to locate existing research. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT an ethical concern when using health information systems?

options.A: Accidentally exposing sensitive patient data in search logs
options.B: Giving free hospital cafeteria coupons to patients
options.C: Algorithm bias that promotes low-quality research studies
options.D: Information overload from poorly filtered search results

explanation: Cafeteria coupons are unrelated to information retrieval ethics, whereas data privacy, algorithmic bias, and information overload are major concerns. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h8)

question: Why must nurses avoid typing patient-identifying details into public or unsecured search tools?

options.A: Search engines are unable to process medical words
options.B: The computer will instantly delete all nursing research files
options.C: Public search engines will charge the hospital a heavy fine
options.D: It violates patient data privacy and confidentiality ethics

explanation: Protecting patient identity is a core nursing duty, and entering identifiable health data into unsecured tools risks privacy breaches. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h8)
